claims.text: The initial high-entropy nanoalloy is a single-phase, equiatomic solid solution containing five or more elements.
Atoms are randomly distributed in the initial nanoalloy.
High-temperature annealing induces preferential surface segregation of oxidation-resistant or refractory elements.
The segregated elements form a thin protective surface layer.
The bulk maintains a random atomic distribution during high-temperature treatment.
High configurational entropy reduces the driving force for phase segregation.
High configurational entropy slows atomic diffusion.
Selective surface segregation creates a passivating layer that suppresses oxidation.
The passivating surface layer suppresses sintering.
Configurational entropy and selective surface segregation act synergistically to stabilize nanoscale structure and chemical composition under high-temperature stress.
After high-temperature treatment, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit minimal grain growth.
After high-temperature treatment, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Under identical thermal conditions, the high-entropy nanoalloy will oxidize less than comparable binary, ternary, or other low-entropy nanoalloys.
Comparable lower-complexity nanoalloys will show significant grain growth under the same high-temperature conditions.
Comparable lower-complexity nanoalloys will undergo phase segregation under the same high-temperature conditions.
Comparable lower-complexity nanoalloys will exhibit greater oxidation under the same high-temperature conditions.
The stability prediction applies approximately from 600 to 1000 degrees Celsius.
At sufficiently high temperatures or long annealing durations, rapid diffusion may overwhelm entropy and surface-segregation stabilization and cause structural degradation.
